method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Assessment and investigation should not delay factor replacement. Discuss every child with haemophilia and bleeding with a haemophilia treatment centre.**
claims.source_text: Assessment and investigation should not delay factor replacement … All children with haemophilia and bleeding should be discussed with a haemophilia treatment centre
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Plan with a haematologist before any procedure** (e.g. lumbar puncture). **Arterial and lumbar puncture only after factor replacement. No IM injections.**
claims.source_text: A haemophilia treatment plan should be made, in consultation with a Haematologist, before performing any procedure (eg lumbar puncture) … Invasive procedures such as arterial puncture and lumbar puncture must only be performed after clotting factor replacement Do not give IM injections
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Haemophilia A = Factor VIII deficiency; B = Factor IX deficiency.** X-linked, affecting 1 in 6,000–10,000 males and under 1 in 300,000 females.
claims.source_text: Haemophilia is an X-linked bleeding disorder affecting 1 in 6,000–10,000 males and less than 1 in 300,000 females … Haemophilia A is clotting Factor VIII (8) deficiency Haemophilia B is clotting Factor IX (9) deficiency
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **History:** mechanism of each injury (internal and joint injuries are often missed); type of haemophilia, treatment plan and inhibitor status; home prophylaxis and time of last dose.
claims.source_text: Elicit a detailed description of each type and mechanism of injury. Internal and joint injuries are often missed … Determine the type of haemophilia (Factor VIII or IX); the child's clotting factor treatment plan and if there are Factor VIII/IX inhibitors … Check if the child is on a home prophylaxis program and when the most recent treatment was administered
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Major or suspected bleeding in the head, neck, chest, GI tract, abdomen or pelvis: give clotting factor immediately**, before a full assessment is complete.
claims.source_text: Major or suspected bleeding in the head, neck, chest, gastrointestinal tract and abdomen and/or pelvis should be treated with clotting factor immediately, before a full assessment is complete
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severity by factor level:** **severe under 1%** — frequent, often spontaneous joint and muscle bleeds · **moderate 1–5%** — bleeds after minor injury, severe bleeds with moderate trauma or surgery · **mild over 5–40%** — bleeds with major trauma such as surgery.
claims.source_text: Severity Concentration of Clotting Factor (%) Typical Bleeding Picture Severe <1 Frequent bleed episodes are common; predominantly into joints & muscles. Bleeding can occur spontaneously or after a minor injury Moderate 1–5 Can bleed after a minor injury. May have bleeding into joints. Severe bleeds occur with moderate trauma, surgery & invasive procedures Mild >5–40 Bleeding occurs with major traumas such as surgery & invasive procedures
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not delay factor replacement for investigations. Routine coagulation studies are not required**; imaging depends on the mechanism of injury.
claims.source_text: Clotting factor replacement should not be delayed by investigations Imaging of the site of suspected bleeding is dependent on the mechanism of injury (trauma) Routine coagulation studies are not required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Emicizumab (Hemlibra) makes standard coagulation tests inaccurate** — do not use them to monitor APTT, factor VIII or factor VIII inhibitor.
claims.source_text: Note: Emicizumab (Hemlibra) affects coagulation testing. Standard coagulation testing will not be accurate and should not be used to monitor APTT, factor VIII or factor VIII inhibitor
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider FBE and ferritin** after recurrent mucosal bleeding — iron deficiency is common.
claims.source_text: Consider FBE and ferritin in children with a history of recurrent mucosal bleeding, as iron deficiency is common
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most bleeds need factor replacement**, except minor soft-tissue injuries and bruising that do not affect function or mobility. **Prompt replacement reduces pain and long-term harm.**
claims.source_text: Most bleeds will require factor replacement with the exception of minor soft tissue injuries and bruising that does not impact on function or mobility Prompt clotting factor replacement reduces the pain and long-term consequences of bleeding
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not delay factor replacement in severe or life-threatening bleeding. Recombinant concentrates are the product of choice.**
claims.source_text: Do not delay clotting factor replacement in severe or life-threatening bleeding Recombinant clotting factor concentrates are the product of choice.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Round doses up to whole vials** — e.g. a 20 kg child needing 30 units/kg factor VIII gets 750 units.
claims.source_text: Doses should be rounded up to use whole vials, eg 20 kg child requiring 30 units/kg factor VIII, give 750 units
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In an emergency any brand of recombinant FVIII is acceptable**, though children should ideally stay on their established brand.
claims.source_text: Whilst it is recommended that children maintain treatment with their established brand of FVIII product, in an emergency situation administration of any brand of recombinant FVIII is acceptable
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Ongoing bleeding despite adequate replacement → suspect a new inhibitor**, especially if previously responsive. **Proven or suspected inhibitors need a bypassing agent.**
claims.source_text: If there is ongoing bleeding after adequate factor replacement, consider that the patient has developed a factor inhibitor and treat accordingly … The presence of a new inhibitor should be suspected in any child who fails to respond clinically to adequate factor replacement, particularly if the child has been previously responsive If the child has factor inhibitors (proven or suspected), a special product is required to ’bypass’ the inhibitor to initiate clotting ie a bypassing agent
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Concentrates are not stocked in every hospital**; regional and rural children should have management plans and ready access to blood products.
claims.source_text: As clotting factor concentrates are not routinely available in all hospitals, children in regional or rural areas should have management plans and ready access to blood products
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Joint and muscle bleeds: start P.R.I.C.E on arrival** — Protection (immobilise), Rest, Ice, gentle Compression, Elevation.
claims.source_text: For muscle and joint bleeds P.R.I.C.E will limit bleeding and reduce pain. Initiate on arrival P = Protection (immobilise the affected area in a position of comfort eg splint/slings/crutches) R = Rest I = Ice (apply a cold pack to reduce bleeding and pain) C = Compression bandage (gentle) E = Elevation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Venepuncture: press for at least 3 minutes afterwards**; minimise failed or distressing attempts (distraction, consider nitrous oxide). IV cannulas are generally not left in on discharge unless discussed with a specialist.
claims.source_text: Children with haemophilia are at risk of venepuncture related bleeding. Treat veins with care, apply pressure for at least 3 minutes post venepuncture In general, IV cannulas are not left insitu on discharge unless discussed with specialist … minimisation of unsuccessful or distressing venepuncture is essential Use distraction and relaxation techniques and consider nitrous oxide sedation.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **No aspirin or NSAIDs** (e.g. ibuprofen, diclofenac). Paracetamol may suffice; opiates for severe pain; splinting helps.
claims.source_text: Do not use products containing aspirin or NSAIDS (eg ibuprofen, diclofenac) as they may worsen bleeding Paracetamol may be sufficient. Opiates can be used for severe pain Splinting and immobilisation is an effective adjunct for reducing pain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider transfer** for care beyond local comfort, or any of: suspected intracranial haemorrhage · neck/throat bleeding · forearm or calf bleed at risk of compartment syndrome · hip or inguinal bleeding (iliopsoas risk) · undiagnosed abdominal pain · persistent haematuria · bleeding causing severe pain.
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when Child requiring care beyond the level of comfort of the local hospital or treating medical team Assessing any child with any of: suspected intracranial haemorrhage bleeding into neck/throat forearm/calf bleed at risk of compartment syndrome bleeding into hip or inguinal area (due to risk of iliopsoas haemorrhage) undiagnosed abdominal pain persistent haematuria bleeding causing severe pain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when** there is no active bleeding, follow-up is arranged and the child has a management plan (e.g. Haemophilia Centre Treatment Card).
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when No active bleeding Appropriate follow-up is arranged Children are provided with a management plan eg Haemophilia Centre Treatment Card
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Haemophilia' (Last updated May 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Haemophilia/, retrieved 2026-09-23
